Chapter: Chapter 3: Mise en Bouche
Caption: Schematic comparison of local (finite element) and global (spectral) basis functions. The finite element "hat function" is non-zero only over two adjacent elements, while the spectral basis function oscillates across the entire domain.
Alt Text: Side-by-side schematic comparing the support of finite element and spectral basis functions. The left panel shows a finite element hat function: a piecewise-linear triangular spike that is nonzero only over two adjacent mesh elements (marked along a tick-spaced axis) and zero everywhere else, labeled local support. The right panel shows a spectral basis function: a high-frequency polynomial that oscillates up and down across the entire domain, labeled global support. The contrast conveys that finite element bases act locally while spectral bases influence the solution everywhere.

Chapter: Chapter 3: Mise en Bouche
Caption: Three strategies for improving accuracy in numerical methods. Spectral methods employ $p$-refinement: increasing the polynomial degree while using a single element (or few elements) spanning the entire domain.
Alt Text: A three-column schematic illustrating refinement strategies, each showing a before state above and an after state below joined by a downward arrow. Left, h-refinement: a coarse two-cell mesh becomes a finer four-cell mesh of equal-width elements, labeled smaller elements. Middle, r-refinement: a uniform four-cell mesh becomes one with the same number of cells redistributed so points cluster on the sides, labeled adaptive redistribution. Right, p-refinement: a low-degree curve labeled p equals two becomes a high-degree oscillating curve labeled p equals eight on the same single element, labeled higher polynomial degree, which is the strategy spectral methods use.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: The Runge phenomenon: polynomial interpolation of $f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2)$ on equispaced nodes. As the polynomial degree increases, oscillations near the boundaries $x = plus.minus 1$ grow unboundedly. The exact function (solid) and interpolants (dashed) are shown for $N = 6$, $10$, and $14$.
Alt Text: Line plot on the interval from minus one to one comparing the smooth bell-shaped Runge function (solid curve) against its polynomial interpolants (dashed curves) on equispaced nodes for degrees six, ten, and fourteen. The interpolants track the function in the center but develop progressively larger oscillations near the endpoints at x equals plus or minus one, with the swings ballooning as the degree rises, illustrating divergence.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Equipotential curves in the complex plane. Left: uniform node density (equispaced nodes). Right: Chebyshev density, where equipotentials are Bernstein ellipses. The poles of the Runge function at $z = plus.minus 0.2 i$ are marked with crosses. For Chebyshev interpolation, the critical ellipse passing through the poles determines the convergence rate.
Alt Text: Two side-by-side contour maps of the complex plane showing closed equipotential curves wrapping the real interval from minus one to one. Left, for uniform equispaced node density, the contours bulge only slightly off the real axis before reaching the Runge poles at z equals plus or minus zero point two i (marked by crosses). Right, for Chebyshev density, the equipotentials are nested Bernstein ellipses with foci at plus or minus one; the critical ellipse passing through the poles sets the convergence rate, and the contours enclose more of the plane, explaining why Chebyshev interpolation converges.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Geometric construction of Chebyshev points. Points equally spaced on the upper semicircle (by angle $theta_j = j pi / N$) project vertically onto the Chebyshev nodes on the $x$-axis. Equal spacing on the circle maps to clustering near the endpoints $x = plus.minus 1$.
Alt Text: Geometric diagram of a unit semicircle with equally spaced points placed along its upper arc at angles theta sub j equal to j pi over N. Vertical dashed projection lines drop each circle point straight down to the x-axis, producing the Chebyshev nodes. Equal angular spacing on the arc maps to nodes that bunch together near the endpoints at x equals plus or minus one and spread out near the center, illustrating endpoint clustering.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Chebyshev interpolation of the Runge function. Left: the function and interpolants for $N = 6$, $10$, and $14$. Right: interpolation error on a logarithmic scale. Unlike equispaced interpolation, the error decreases rapidly with increasing $N$.
Alt Text: Two-panel figure on Chebyshev interpolation of the Runge function. Left, a line plot from minus one to one shows the function and its interpolants for degrees six, ten, and fourteen lying almost on top of the function with no boundary oscillations. Right, the pointwise interpolation error on a logarithmic vertical axis drops sharply as the degree increases, the opposite of the equispaced case, confirming rapid convergence.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Lagrange basis polynomials $L_k (x)$ for $N = 10$. Left: equispaced nodes show large oscillations near the boundaries. Right: Chebyshev nodes yield bounded basis functions throughout the interval.
Alt Text: Two side-by-side line plots of the Lagrange basis polynomials L sub k for degree ten over the interval minus one to one, each curve equal to one at its own node and zero at the others. Left, on equispaced nodes the basis functions belonging to interior nodes swing to large positive and negative values near the boundaries. Right, on Chebyshev nodes every basis function stays small and bounded across the whole interval, showing far better behavior.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Left: Lebesgue functions $Lambda_(N)(x)$ for $N = 10$ with equispaced, Legendre, and Chebyshev nodes. The equispaced case has large peaks near the boundaries. Right: Growth of Lebesgue constants with $N$. The equispaced constant grows exponentially, while Chebyshev grows only logarithmically.
Alt Text: Two-panel figure on Lebesgue functions and constants. Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Lebesgue constants for Legendre and Chebyshev nodes (equispaced omitted for clarity). Chebyshev nodes achieve the slowest possible growth rate $O(ln N)$, while Legendre nodes grow as $O(sqrt(N))$. Both are far superior to equispaced nodes, but Chebyshev remains the optimal choice.
Alt Text: Semilogarithmic plot of the Lebesgue constant versus polynomial degree N comparing only Legendre and Chebyshev nodes, with the divergent equispaced curve omitted. The Legendre curve rises faster, consistent with order square root of N growth, while the Chebyshev curve grows most slowly, consistent with order log N, confirming Chebyshev nodes as the optimal choice among the two.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Convergence comparison for the Runge function. The maximum interpolation error is plotted against polynomial degree $N$ on a semilogarithmic scale. Chebyshev interpolation (green) converges at rate $O(rho^(-N))$ with $rho approx 1.22$. Equispaced interpolation (red) diverges exponentially.
Alt Text: Semilogarithmic convergence plot of the maximum interpolation error against polynomial degree N for the Runge function. Chapter: Chapter 4: The Geometry of Nodes
Caption: Chebyshev interpolation convergence for the Runge function (equispaced omitted for clarity). The error decreases geometrically at rate $O(rho^(-N))$ with $rho approx 1.22$, matching the theoretical prediction based on the pole locations at $z = plus.minus 0.2 i$.
Alt Text: Semilogarithmic plot of the maximum Chebyshev interpolation error versus polynomial degree N for the Runge function, shown alone without the divergent equispaced curve. The error markers fall along a near-perfect descending straight line, the signature of geometric convergence at rate rho to the power minus N with rho about one point two two, matching the theoretical prediction from the pole locations at z equals plus or minus zero point two i.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Finite difference stencils in one dimension, progressing from local to global. The derivative at the central node $x_i$ (red) is approximated using only the highlighted nodes (blue) within each stencil. From top to bottom: 3-point stencil (2nd order), 5-point stencil (4th order), 7-point stencil (6th order), and spectral method (all nodes). As the stencil widens, accuracy improves. The spectral method represents the limiting case where _every_ node contributes to the derivative approximation, yielding exponential rather than algebraic convergence.
Alt Text: Four stacked one-dimensional node rows on a number line illustrate widening finite-difference stencils. In each row the central node x-i is marked red and the nodes contributing to its derivative are marked blue: a 3-point stencil (second order), then 5-point (fourth order), then 7-point (sixth order), and finally the spectral method, where every node on the line is highlighted. The takeaway is that a broader stencil raises accuracy, and the spectral case is the limit in which all nodes contribute, giving exponential rather than algebraic convergence.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Sparsity patterns of differentiation matrices for $N = 20$ grid points. Left: second-order finite differences (tridiagonal, bandwidth 3). Center: fourth-order finite differences (pentadiagonal, bandwidth 5). Right: spectral method (dense, bandwidth $N$). The progression illustrates the key insight: spectral methods are the limiting case of finite differences as the stencil width extends to the full domain.
Alt Text: Three side-by-side matrix sparsity patterns for twenty grid points, with nonzero entries shown as filled cells. Left: second-order finite differences form a narrow tridiagonal band of width three. Center: fourth-order finite differences form a pentadiagonal band of width five. Right: the spectral matrix is completely dense, with every off-diagonal entry filled. The sequence shows spectral methods as the limit of finite differences when the stencil spans the whole domain.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Periodic cardinal functions $phi_j (x)$ for $N = 16$ equispaced nodes on $[0, 2 pi)$. Each function peaks at value $1$ at its corresponding node $x_j$ and vanishes at all other nodes, satisfying the cardinal property $phi_j (x_k) = delta_(j k)$. The oscillations decay smoothly away from each peak, in contrast to the boundary-amplified oscillations seen in Lagrange basis polynomials for non-periodic interpolation.
Alt Text: Overlaid curves of periodic cardinal functions phi-j on the interval zero to two pi for sixteen equispaced nodes. Each smooth oscillating curve rises to a value of one at its own node and crosses zero at every other node, satisfying the cardinal property. The oscillations damp smoothly with distance from each peak, with no growth toward the domain ends, unlike the boundary-amplified oscillations of Lagrange polynomials in non-periodic interpolation.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Structure of the periodic spectral differentiation matrix for $N = 16$. _Left_: heatmap showing the matrix entries. The Toeplitz (constant diagonal) structure is evident, as is the skew-symmetry ($D^top = -D$) with positive values (red) appearing where negative values (blue) appear in the transpose. _Right_: the first row entries $D_(0,k)$ (blue dots) plotted against the column offset $k = j - i$. The dashed red curve shows the continuous cotangent function $1/2 dot (-1)^k cot(k pi / N)$ from @eq-spectral-periodic, confirming that the discrete matrix entries lie exactly on this curve. The antisymmetric pattern ($D_(0,k) = -D_(0,-k)$) reflects the skew-symmetry of~$D$.
Alt Text: Two panels characterizing the periodic spectral differentiation matrix for sixteen points. Left: a color heatmap of the matrix entries showing constant-diagonal Toeplitz structure and skew-symmetry, with red positive values mirrored by blue negative values across the diagonal. Right: a scatter plot of the first-row entries D-zero-k against column offset k, with blue dots lying exactly on a dashed red curve given by one half times minus-one to the power k times cotangent of k pi over N, and an antisymmetric shape confirming the skew-symmetry.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Spectral differentiation of $u(x) = e^(sin^2 x)$ using $N = 64$ grid points. Left: the function $u$ (navy) and its first derivative $u'$ exact (coral) vs. spectral (teal circles). Right: second derivative $u''$ exact (purple) vs. spectral (teal squares). The maximum errors, displayed in each panel, are near machine precision ($approx 10^(-14)$). This remarkable accuracy with relatively few points is the hallmark of spectral methods for smooth periodic functions.
Alt Text: Two panels showing spectral differentiation of u of x equals e to the power sine squared x with sixty-four points. Left: the navy function curve together with its first derivative, where the exact coral curve and the teal circle markers coincide. Right: the second derivative, with the exact purple curve and teal square markers coinciding. Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Fornberg's recursive algorithm visualized as a "stencil pyramid." Each box represents a weight $delta_m^((k, n))$ for node index $k$ in a stencil of $n + 1$ nodes. The algorithm builds from top (single node) to bottom (full stencil). Green arrows indicate updates to existing node weights via @eq-fornberg-old; red arrows show computation of new node weights via @eq-fornberg-new. The recursive structure ensures numerical stability.
Alt Text: Triangular diagram of Fornberg's recursive algorithm drawn as a stencil pyramid. Each row is one level holding boxes that represent weights delta for node index k in a stencil of n plus one nodes, with the single-node top widening to the full stencil at the bottom. Green arrows show updates to existing node weights and red arrows show computation of each newly added node's weight, and the layered dependencies illustrate why the recursion is numerically stable.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Differentiation Matrices
Caption: Differentiation error comparison: finite differences versus spectral method. The test function is $u(x) = 1/(2 + sin(x))$ on the periodic domain $[0, 2pi)$. Finite difference methods (FD2, FD4, FD6) exhibit algebraic convergence with the expected rates $O(N^(-2))$, $O(N^(-4))$, $O(N^(-6))$. The spectral method achieves geometric (exponential) convergence, reaching near machine precision around $N = 50$. Dashed lines show theoretical convergence rates.
Alt Text: Semilogarithmic plot of differentiation error versus grid size N, with error on a logarithmic vertical axis and N on a linear horizontal axis, for the test function one over two plus sine x. The three finite-difference curves, labelled FD2, FD4, and FD6, bend downward with progressively steeper algebraic slopes matching N to the minus two, minus four, and minus six, shown against dashed reference lines. The spectral curve falls as a straight line, reaching near machine precision around N equals fifty, dramatically outperforming the finite-difference schemes.

Caption: Higher-order spectral derivatives of $u(x) = e^(-sin(2x))$ using $N = 32$ grid points. Chapter: Chapter 6: Smoothness and Spectral Accuracy
Caption: The smoothness hierarchysmoothness hierarchy and corresponding Fourier decay rates. More smoothness implies faster decay.
Alt Text: A three-column reference table listing smoothness classes against their Fourier-coefficient decay rates and a representative example for each, ranging from bounded-variation functions decaying like one over k up to band-limited functions with compactly supported spectra; the takeaway is that greater smoothness yields progressively faster decay.

Chapter: Chapter 6: Smoothness and Spectral Accuracy
Caption: The decay hierarchy of Fourier coefficients. Functions with greater smoothness exhibit faster decay: algebraic ($O(k^(-4))$) for finite regularity, geometric ($O(e^(-alpha k))$) for strip-analytic functions, and super-geometric for entire functions. The plot shows $|hat(f)_k|$ versus wavenumber $k$ on a semi-log scale.
Alt Text: A semi-log plot of Fourier-coefficient magnitude versus wavenumber k for three test functions, with the vertical axis logarithmic and the horizontal axis linear. The piecewise-smooth absolute-sine-cubed function gives a slowly bending downward curve (algebraic decay like k to the power minus four), the strip-analytic one over one-plus-sine-squared traces a nearly straight descending line (geometric decay), and the entire function e to the sine of x falls off faster than any straight line (super-geometric decay), cleanly separating the three smoothness regimes.

Chapter: Chapter 6: Smoothness and Spectral Accuracy
Caption: The aliasing phenomenon. _Left_: A function $f(x) = sin(x) + 0.5 sin(10 x)$ sampled at $N = 12$ points. The high-frequency component $sin(10 x)$ aliases to $sin(-2 x)$, producing a misleading interpolant. _Center_: Frequency folding diagram showing how wavenumbers $k = 10$ and $k = -10$ fold into the resolved range $[-6, 6]$. _Right_: True versus aliased spectrum for $f(x) = 1/(1.5 + cos(x))$.
Alt Text: A three-panel illustration of aliasing. Left: a sine plus a higher-frequency sine sampled at only twelve points, where an interpolant drawn through the samples follows a misleading low-frequency curve rather than the true rapid oscillation. Center: a frequency-folding diagram showing how wavenumbers ten and minus ten outside the resolvable band fold back into the range minus six to six. Right: a comparison of the true spectrum computed from many samples against the aliased spectrum from few samples, where unresolved high modes contaminate the low ones.

Chapter: Chapter 6: Smoothness and Spectral Accuracy
Caption: Spectral differentiation convergence rates for three functions of increasing smoothness. The error is measured in the maximum norm $norm(f' - D bold(f))_infinity$. Functions with greater smoothness achieve faster convergence, exactly as predicted by Theorem 4.
Alt Text: A semi-log convergence plot with maximum-norm spectral differentiation error on the logarithmic vertical axis versus the number of grid points N on the horizontal axis, for three functions of increasing smoothness. The only-twice-differentiable absolute-sine-cubed function declines slowly along an algebraic trend like N to the power minus three; the strip-analytic one over one-plus-sine-squared falls as a straight line indicating geometric convergence; and the entire function e to the sine of x plunges almost vertically to machine precision near N equals thirty, demonstrating super-geometric convergence as predicted by the differentiation theorem.

Bottom right: the polynomial $x^8$ is differentiated exactly for $N gt.eq.slant 8$.

The FFT-based approach uses the Chebyshev--Fourier connection. The tensor-product form $D_2 U + U D_2^top$ achieves $O(N^3)$ without explicit Kronecker products.
Alt Text: Table comparing the computational complexity of matrix-based versus FFT-based spectral differentiation for first and second one-dimensional derivatives and the two-dimensional Laplacian, showing the FFT approach reaching N log N or N squared log N cost where dense matrices need N squared, N cubed, or N to the fourth.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Spectral convergence of Fourier differentiation for the test function $u(x) = e^(sin x)$. Both the matrix approach ($D bold(u)$) and the FFT approach ($cal(F)^(-1)(i k hat(u))$) achieve machine precision for $N gt.eq.slant 30$, confirming that the two methods are algebraically equivalent.
Alt Text: Semilog convergence plot for differentiating e to the power sine x on a periodic grid: the horizontal axis is the number of grid points N (linear) and the vertical axis is the maximum error (logarithmic). Two overlapping curves, one for the dense circulant matrix and one for the FFT route, fall exponentially with N and flatten near ten to the power minus fifteen for N at or above thirty, showing the two methods are numerically identical and both reach machine precision.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Computational cost of Fourier differentiation. The dense matrix approach scales as $O(N^2)$; the FFT approach as $O(N log N)$. For $N = 2048$ the FFT is roughly 1000 times faster.
Alt Text: Log-log timing plot with the grid size N on the horizontal axis and wall-clock time on the vertical axis. The dense matrix curve rises as a steep straight line of slope two (order N squared), while the FFT curve rises much more gently (order N log N); the widening vertical gap shows the FFT becoming about a thousand times faster by N equal to two thousand forty-eight.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Fourier pseudospectral versus second-order upwind finite differences for linear advection after one full period ($t = 2 pi$, $N = 128$). _Left_: The spectral solution (blue) is visually indistinguishable from the exact initial condition. Left panel plots the solution profile versus x: the blue Fourier spectral curve sits exactly on the exact Gaussian pulse, while the red dashed second-order upwind finite-difference curve is broadened and lagged by numerical dispersion and dissipation. Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation @eq-ks with $L = 32 pi$: the space-time "fingerprint" of spatiotemporal chaos. The initial random perturbation develops into a pattern of merging and splitting cellular structures, a hallmark of the KS dynamics. The per-step IF-RK4 handles the severe stiffness ($lambda_k tilde.op k^4$) without difficulty.
Alt Text: Space-time color map of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation on a domain of length thirty-two pi, with x on the horizontal axis and time on the vertical axis. After a brief transient the field settles into a statistically steady pattern of cellular stripes that continually merge and split, the characteristic fingerprint of spatiotemporal chaos handled stably despite the strong fourth-derivative stiffness.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Time-averaged energy spectrum of the KS equation in the statistically steady chaotic regime. Energy is concentrated at low wavenumbers (the linearly unstable range $|k| < 1$) and decays rapidly at high wavenumbers due to the fourth-derivative damping.
Alt Text: Time-averaged energy spectrum of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation in its chaotic steady state, plotting energy versus wavenumber on a logarithmic scale. Energy peaks at low wavenumbers within the linearly unstable band where the magnitude of k is below one, then falls off steeply toward high wavenumbers as the fourth-derivative term damps small scales.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: 2D Navier--Stokes: decaying turbulence on $[0, 2 pi)^2$ with $nu = 10^(-3)$ and $N = 128$. Vorticity snapshots at $t = 0$, $5$, $10$, and $20$. Small-scale structures merge into large coherent vortices, demonstrating the inverse energy cascade characteristic of two-dimensional turbulence.
Alt Text: Four vorticity snapshots of two-dimensional decaying turbulence on the periodic square zero to two pi, with viscosity ten to the power minus three and N equal to one hundred twenty-eight, shown at times zero, five, ten, and twenty. Each is a color map of vorticity over the plane; the initially fine-grained field of many small positive and negative vortices progressively merges into a few large coherent vortex blobs, illustrating the inverse energy cascade.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Fourier Pseudospectral Methods for Periodic PDEs
Caption: Diagnostics for 2D decaying turbulence. _Left_: Kinetic energy $E(t) = frac(1, 2) chevron.l |bold(u)|^2 chevron.r$ decays slowly as energy cascades to large scales and is eventually dissipated. _Right_: Enstrophy $Z(t) = frac(1, 2) chevron.l omega^2 chevron.r$ decays much faster, consistent with the selective decay principle of two-dimensional turbulence.
Alt Text: Two-panel diagnostics for two-dimensional decaying turbulence, both plotting a quantity versus time. Left panel shows kinetic energy declining slowly and gradually as energy moves to large scales. Right panel shows enstrophy, the mean squared vorticity, decaying much more steeply and rapidly, consistent with the selective decay principle in which enstrophy is dissipated far faster than energy.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Two spectral grids on the unit disk with $N_r = 25$ radial and $M = 20$ angular points. _Left_: the naive grid maps Chebyshev points to $r in [0, 1]$, resulting in heavy clustering near the origin. The dashed circle (containing half the grid points) encloses only 25% of the disk area. _Right_: the doubled grid uses Chebyshev points on $r in [-1, 1]$ with odd $N_r$, keeping only the positive-$r$ half. No point falls at the origin, and the resolution is more uniformly distributed.
Alt Text: Two side-by-side scatter plots of grid points on the unit disk, each with twenty-five radial and twenty angular points. The left panel, the naive grid, shows points densely clustered in a tight knot around the centre, with a dashed circle marking where half the points lie yet enclosing only a quarter of the disk area. The right panel, the doubled grid, spreads points far more evenly across the disk with no point at the origin, illustrating that the doubling trick distributes resolution efficiently.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: _Left_: area of each radial annulus for the naive and doubled grids. The naive grid allocates disproportionate area to the thin annuli near $r = 0$. _Right_: CFL time-step scaling. The naive grid forces $Delta t_(max) tilde.op N_r^(-4)$ (blue circles), while the doubled grid gives $Delta t_(max) tilde.op N_r^(-2)$ (red squares), a substantial improvement.
Alt Text: Two panels comparing the naive and doubled radial grids. The left panel plots annulus area against radial position, showing the naive grid wastes area on extremely thin annuli near the centre while the doubled grid keeps areas balanced. The right panel is a log-log plot of maximum stable time step versus radial point count, where blue circles for the naive grid fall along a steep slope of minus four and red squares for the doubled grid follow a gentler slope of minus two, demonstrating a far less restrictive time-step constraint.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Six eigenmodes of the Laplacian on the unit disk, computed with $N_r = 25$ radial and $M = 20$ angular points. The modes display the characteristic Bessel function patterns: the fundamental mode ($m = 0$, $n = 1$) is a simple dome, while higher modes exhibit nodal diameters (radial lines) and nodal circles.
Alt Text: A grid of six color-mapped eigenmode patterns of the Laplacian on the unit disk, computed with twenty-five radial and twenty angular points. The fundamental mode is a single smooth dome of one sign, while the remaining modes show increasingly intricate Bessel-type patterns of alternating positive and negative regions separated by nodal diameters (straight node lines through the centre) and concentric nodal circles, matching classical drumhead vibration shapes.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: _Left_: the first 25 computed eigenvalues (circles) agree with the exact Bessel zeros squared (crosses) to plotting accuracy. The degenerate pairs ($m gt.eq.slant 1$) appear as overlapping markers. _Right_: the error in the fundamental eigenvalue $lambda_(0,1)$ decreases exponentially with $N_r$, confirming spectral convergence.
Alt Text: Two panels validating the disk eigenvalues. The left panel plots the first twenty-five eigenvalues by index, with computed circles landing exactly on the exact squared Bessel zeros marked as crosses, and degenerate pairs for angular number at least one appearing as coincident markers. The right panel is a semilog plot of the error in the fundamental eigenvalue against radial point count, showing a straight downward line that signals exponential, spectral convergence to near machine precision.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Nodal line rotation in the first degenerate eigenspace ($lambda approx 14.68$). As the mixing angle $phi$ varies, the single nodal diameter rotates continuously through the disk. The faint background shading shows the sign of the eigenmode (red positive, blue negative). This continuous family of modes reflects the underlying rotational symmetry of the circular domain.
Alt Text: A sequence of disk plots showing the single nodal diameter of the first degenerate eigenspace at eigenvalue approximately fourteen point sixty-eight. As the mixing angle phi increases, the straight node line rotates smoothly to successive orientations across the disk, over faint red and blue background shading marking positive and negative regions of the mode. The continuous rotation illustrates that any orientation is an equally valid eigenmode, reflecting the rotational symmetry of the circle.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Three-dimensional surface plot of the Poisson solution on the unit disk with the off-centre Gaussian load @eq-gaussian-source. The membrane deflects most strongly near the load position $(0.4, 0.2)$, with the deflection smoothly decaying to zero at the clamped boundary $r = 1$.
Alt Text: A three-dimensional surface plot of the Poisson solution, the deflection of a clamped circular membrane under an off-centre Gaussian load. The surface rises to a single rounded peak located over the load position at x equals zero point four, y equals zero point two, then falls away smoothly in all directions to zero at the circular clamped rim, showing the asymmetric response to the off-centre forcing.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Filled contour plot of the Poisson solution. The red star marks the centre of the Gaussian load. The equipotential lines (level curves) are distorted toward the load location, reflecting the broken radial symmetry.
Alt Text: A filled contour plot of the Poisson solution over the unit disk, with color indicating deflection magnitude. A red star marks the centre of the Gaussian load, and the level curves form roughly concentric loops crowded and shifted toward the load location rather than centred on the origin, visibly distorted away from circular symmetry by the off-centre source.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates
Caption: Radial profiles $u(r, theta_k)$ at eight equally spaced angles $theta_k$, with $r = 1$ (clamped boundary) on the left and $r arrow 0$ (origin) on the right. All profiles vanish at $r = 1$ by the homogeneous Dirichlet condition. _Left_: for the centred source ($x_0 = y_0 = 0$), all eight profiles are indistinguishable to machine precision, collapsing onto a single monotone curve that peaks near the origin. This exact collapse — not merely visual agreement — confirms that the spectral discretisation introduces no artificial anisotropy. _Right_: for the off-centre source at $(0.4, 0.2)$, the profiles fan out. The source lies at radial distance $r_s = sqrt(0.4^2 + 0.2^2) approx 0.45$ from the origin and at angle $theta_s = arctan(0.2 / 0.4) approx 0.46$ rad. The orange profile ($theta approx 0.63$ rad, the sampled angle nearest to the source direction) peaks near $r approx 0.45$, consistent with the source distance. Profiles at angles pointing away from the source remain substantially lower throughout, and all profiles reconverge to zero as $r arrow 1$.
Alt Text: Two panels of radial profiles of the solution at eight equally spaced angles, plotted from the clamped boundary at radius one on the left to the origin on the right, all vanishing at the boundary. In the left panel, for a centred source, the eight curves collapse exactly onto one monotone curve peaking at the origin, confirming no artificial anisotropy. In the right panel, for the off-centre source at zero point four, zero point two, the curves fan apart; the profile nearest the source direction peaks near radius zero point four-five at the source distance, while profiles pointing away stay much lower, and all return to zero at the boundary.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Spectral Methods in Polar Coordinates

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Inhomogeneous Poisson equation @eq-inhom-poisson solved by lifting. _Left_: the numerical solution (circles) agrees with the reference solution for $N = 16$. _Right_: the maximum error decreases exponentially with $N$, reaching machine precision by $N approx 20$.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Helmholtz equation @eq-helmholtz-robin with Robin boundary condition @eq-helmholtz-robin-bc for $k = 2$ and $N = 32$. _Left_: solutions for $alpha = 0$ (Neumann), $alpha = 1$, $alpha = 5$, and $alpha = 20$. The left panel plots solution u against x for four values of the Robin parameter alpha equal to zero (Neumann), one, five, and twenty; as alpha increases the curves are progressively pulled down toward zero at the left endpoint x equal to minus one, showing the smooth transition from Neumann toward Dirichlet behaviour. Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Condition number of the discrete Helmholtz operator with Robin boundary condition as a function of $alpha$ for $N = 16$, $32$, and $64$. The condition number is moderate for all practical values of $alpha$ and grows polynomially with $N$, as expected for spectral differentiation matrices.
Alt Text: Semilog plot of the condition number of the discrete Robin Helmholtz operator against the Robin parameter alpha, with three curves for N equal to sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four. Each curve stays at a moderate level across the full range of alpha, with the larger N giving uniformly larger condition numbers, illustrating that conditioning grows only polynomially with N and depends only mildly on alpha, so the tau row-replacement approach remains numerically robust.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Allen--Cahn equation @eq-allen-cahn-bc with fixed Dirichlet conditions $u(plus.minus 1) = plus.minus 1$ and $epsilon = 0.01$. Alt Text: Space-time color map of the Allen-Cahn solution with fixed Dirichlet boundaries at minus one and plus one and small parameter epsilon equal to zero point zero one, with horizontal axis position x and vertical axis time. Three nearly vertical transition layers separating the plus and minus phases appear at the start and persist almost unchanged for a long interval, the metastable regime, until near time forty-five two of the interfaces abruptly merge and annihilate, leaving a single central interface fixed by the boundary data.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Allen--Cahn equation with time-dependent right boundary $u(1, t) = 1 + sin^2(t/5)$. The oscillating boundary pumps energy into the domain, shifting the equilibrium interface to $x approx -0.4$ and causing earlier annihilation near $t approx 30$.
Alt Text: Space-time color map of the Allen-Cahn solution with an oscillating right boundary equal to one plus sine squared of t over five, horizontal axis position x and vertical axis time. Compared with the fixed-boundary case, the driven boundary pumps energy in, shifting the surviving equilibrium interface leftward to about x equal to minus zero point four and triggering the annihilation of the extra interfaces earlier, near time thirty.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Radiative cooling problem @eq-radiative-problem with $sigma = 1$ and $N = 32$. _Left_: temperature profiles at $t = 0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5$ showing the approach to steady state. Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Quasinormal mode spectrum for the Pöschl--Teller potential @eq-poschl-teller with $V_0 = 2$, $N = 80$, $L = 8$. Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Eigenfunctions of the first two quasinormal modes. _Left_: the fundamental mode ($n = 0$), showing a single antinode centred on the potential peak. _Right_: the first overtone ($n = 1$), with one nodal crossing. Alt Text: Two panels showing the eigenfunctions of the first two quasinormal modes plotted against position x. The left panel shows the fundamental mode, index n equal to zero, with a single antinode (one main peak) centred on the potential peak at the origin. The right panel shows the first overtone, index n equal to one, with one nodal crossing through zero. In both panels the tails at large absolute x oscillate and grow, reflecting the outgoing and ingoing wave boundary conditions characteristic of quasinormal modes.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods
Caption: Convergence of the fundamental QNM frequency $omega_0$. _Left_: error $|omega_0^("num") - omega_0^("exact")|$ versus $N$ for fixed $L = 8$, showing initial spectral convergence that saturates at $approx 2 times 10^(-4)$ due to domain truncation. _Right_: error versus truncation length $L$ for fixed $N = 80$, showing exponential decay until $L approx 9$, beyond which the grid becomes too coarse to resolve the solution and the error increases again.
Alt Text: Two semilog convergence panels for the fundamental quasinormal frequency omega-zero. The left panel plots the error against the number of points N at fixed truncation length L equal to eight: the error first falls steeply (spectral convergence) but then flattens onto a plateau near two times ten to the power minus four set by domain truncation. The right panel plots the error against truncation length L at fixed N equal to eighty: the error decays exponentially up to about L equal to nine, then turns and rises again as the fixed grid becomes too coarse to resolve the wider domain, revealing an optimal L.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Advanced Boundary Conditions for Spectral Methods

Chapter: Chapter 14: Higher-Order Boundary Value Problems
Caption: Pseudospectra of the Orr--Sommerfeld operator for plane Poiseuille flow with $N = 100$, $R = 5772$, $alpha = 1$. The eigenvalues (dots) lie in the stable half-plane $op("Im")(c) < 0$, but the $epsilon$-pseudospectral contours extend far into the unstable region. The contours at $epsilon = 10^(-2), 10^(-4), 10^(-6), 10^(-8), 10^(-10)$ show that even a tiny perturbation of order $epsilon approx 10^(-4)$ can push an eigenvalue across the stability boundary. This extreme sensitivity --- a consequence of the non-normality of the operator --- explains the subcritical transition to turbulence observed in experiments at $R << R_c$.
Alt Text: A complex-plane contour plot of the epsilon-pseudospectra of the non-normal Orr-Sommerfeld operator at N equals one hundred, Reynolds number five thousand seven hundred seventy-two, wavenumber one. Dots mark the eigenvalues, all lying in the stable lower half-plane (imaginary part of c below zero), while nested level curves for epsilon equal to ten to the power minus two, minus four, minus six, minus eight, and minus ten surround them. The outer contours balloon upward across the imaginary-part-zero stability boundary into the unstable region, showing that a perturbation as small as about ten to the power minus four can make an eigenvalue unstable, the non-normality mechanism behind subcritical transition.

Chapter: Chapter 15: Quadrature in Spectral Methods: When Exactness Misleads

Newton--Cotes (coral) and Clenshaw--Curtis (teal) are exact for $k lt.eq.slant n = 32$ and lift off afterwards; Gauss--Legendre (navy) stays at machine precision throughout because its degree of precision $2n + 1 = 65$ exceeds the entire test range. Odd $k$ are zero by symmetry and have been clamped to the machine-epsilon floor for the log scale.
Alt Text: Semilog plot of monomial quadrature error versus monomial degree k from zero to sixty-four for three rules using thirty-three points. The coral Newton-Cotes and teal Clenshaw-Curtis curves hug the machine-precision floor near ten to the power minus sixteen up to degree thirty-two, then climb steeply once k exceeds n. The navy Gauss-Legendre curve stays flat at the floor across the entire range, since its degree of precision sixty-five exceeds every test degree. Odd-degree points sit on the floor by symmetry.

Chapter: Chapter 15: Quadrature in Spectral Methods: When Exactness Misleads
Caption: Quadrature errors for $f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2)$ on $[-1, 1]$. Newton--Cotes (red) diverges exponentially while Gauss--Legendre (navy) and Clenshaw--Curtis (teal) converge rapidly.

The contrast shows that equal degree of precision does not guarantee accuracy.

Chapter: Chapter 15: Quadrature in Spectral Methods: When Exactness Misleads

Chapter: Chapter 16: Integration of Periodic Functions: Why the Trapezoidal Rule Becomes Spectral

Chapter: Chapter 16: Integration of Periodic Functions: Why the Trapezoidal Rule Becomes Spectral
Caption: (a) Trapezoidal error for a random trigonometric polynomial of degree $m = 10$. Once $N > m$, the rule is exact. Chapter: Chapter 16: Integration of Periodic Functions: Why the Trapezoidal Rule Becomes Spectral

Chapter: Chapter 16: Integration of Periodic Functions: Why the Trapezoidal Rule Becomes Spectral

Chapter: Chapter 16: Integration of Periodic Functions: Why the Trapezoidal Rule Becomes Spectral
Caption: (a) Fourier coefficients $|hat(f)_k|$ of $1/(2 - cos x)$. The exact closed form $r^(|k|) / sqrt(3)$ (navy) and the FFT-computed values from $N = 32$ samples (coral dots) coincide on the plot. (b) The absolute error in each FFT coefficient. In the resolved band the error is at machine precision; near the Nyquist frequency $|k| = N/2$ the error grows because of aliasing tails, but it remains far below the magnitude of the coefficient itself. _Every spectral coefficient computed by the FFT in this textbook is, secretly, an instance of the periodic trapezoidal rule._

Caption: Three deliberate blow-ups. _Left_: Fourier advection with forward Euler and $Delta t$ 20% above the stability threshold; sawtooth oscillations appear at the highest wavenumbers and grow to fill the domain. _Centre_: Chebyshev wave equation with leapfrog and $Delta t$ 50% too large; the instability is localised near the boundaries $x = plus.minus 1$. _Right_: Chebyshev heat equation with forward Euler and $Delta t$ tripled beyond the stability limit; boundary-localised oscillations grow explosively within a few steps. In each case, the instability first appears in the modes associated with the largest eigenvalues of the spatial operator.
Alt Text: Three side-by-side line plots of solution profiles, each showing a deliberate time-stepping blow-up. Left, Fourier advection stepped just above its stability limit, where rapid sawtooth oscillations at the highest wavenumbers have grown to fill the whole domain. Right, the Chebyshev heat equation with forward Euler at triple the stable step, again erupting near the boundaries. The common lesson: instability first strikes the modes tied to the largest eigenvalues of the spatial operator.

Chapter: Chapter 18: Linear Spectral Eigenproblems
Caption: The rational Chebyshev $"TB"_n$ map and basis. _Left_: the algebraic map $x = ell , t / sqrt(1 - t^2)$ for four values of the map parameter $ell$; the asymptotes at $t = plus.minus 1$ (vertical dotted lines) carry $x$ to $plus.minus infinity$. Each $"TB"_n$ asymptotes to a constant at $|x| arrow infinity$ --- exactly the behaviour required to represent functions that decay algebraically or settle to a constant.

Caption: Étude 18.7: manufacturing fake instability. Chapter: Chapter 19: Coordinate Transformations and Mapped Spectral Methods
Caption: Étude 19.5: healing the square-root branch point. _(a)_ The target function in physical coordinates $sqrt(1 - X^2)$ (coral) and in mapped coordinates $"sech" y$ (teal). _(b)_ Pointwise error $|g(X) - g_N (X)|$ at fixed $N = 32$ vs the physical coordinate $X$, plotted on a semilog axis. The étude's verbal claim "the singularity at the endpoint hurts the direct expansion" becomes a quantitative visual fact: the failure is *spatial*, not just integral. _(c)_ Max-norm error vs $N$ on a log-log scale; the direct expansion tracks $1 / N$ (dotted guide line), while the tanh-mapped expansion descends geometrically, reaching $10^(-9)$ at $N = 128$. _(d)_ Chebyshev coefficients at $N = 64$; the direct expansion shows the algebraic envelope $|a_n| tilde.op 1 / n^2$ of the square-root series, while the tanh-mapped expansion is geometric with a decay rate of roughly $exp(-n / 3)$.
Alt Text: Four panels on healing a square-root branch-point singularity. Panel a plots the target square root of one minus X squared in physical coordinates against the smooth sech of y in mapped coordinates. Panel b plots pointwise error at N of thirty-two versus the physical coordinate on a semilog axis: the direct expansion is uniformly poor with sharp peaks at the endpoints X equals plus or minus one, while the tanh-mapped expansion stays near machine precision in the interior and rises only gently near the boundaries. Panel c plots max-norm error versus N on a log-log axis, the direct expansion tracking a one-over-N guide line while the tanh-mapped expansion descends geometrically, reaching about ten to the minus nine at N of one hundred twenty-eight. Panel d plots Chebyshev coefficient magnitudes at N of sixty-four, the direct expansion showing an algebraic one-over-n-squared envelope and the mapped expansion a steep geometric decay.

Chapter: Chapter 19: Coordinate Transformations and Mapped Spectral Methods
Caption: Étude 19.6: square Poisson with corner stress. _Top row, (a)–(c)_: _(a)_ contour plot of the solution at $N = 32$, showing the roughly circular level sets and the mild but unmistakable corner flattening; _(b)_ one-dimensional view of the physical grids at $N = 24$ --- the standard Chebyshev grid (navy) and the tanh-clustered grid with $alpha = 2$ (coral) differ only near the endpoints but differ sharply there; _(c)_ max-norm error against the reference, for the unmapped method and for tanh clustering with $alpha in {1, 2, 3}$. The unmapped method _wins_ at every resolution tested up to $N = 64$, a striking confirmation of Boyd's crossover warning. _Bottom row, (d)–(f)_: pointwise error fields $|u_N - u_("ref")|$ at $N = 24$ on a common log-colour scale, for the unmapped method (d), tanh $alpha = 1$ (e), and tanh $alpha = 3$ (f). Boyd's warning made spatial: aggressive clustering moves the error _away_ from the corners (where it's hard to suppress) and _into_ the interior (where it didn't need to be), without reducing the $ell^infinity$ norm. Total integrated error is roughly conserved by the choice of $alpha$ at this resolution; only at much larger $N$ would the asymptotic singularity-resolution gain finally beat the constant-factor cost of the resampled interior.

Chapter: Chapter 19: Coordinate Transformations and Mapped Spectral Methods
Caption: Étude 19.8: accuracy versus timestep under the Kosloff--Tal-Ezer map. _(a)_ The KTE map $y(xi) = arcsin((1 - beta) xi) / arcsin(1 - beta)$ for the three regimes the étude compares: standard Chebyshev (navy, identity), aggressive $beta tilde.op 1 / N^2$ at $N = 32$ (coral), and conservative $beta = 1 - cos(1 / 2)$ (teal). The CGL nodes $xi_j$ on the bottom show the input grid; the curves' steepness near $xi = plus.minus 1$ measures how strongly the map _flattens_ the boundary clustering. The aggressive curve is nearly straight --- exactly the flattening that buys timestep --- while the conservative one keeps a meaningful S-shape. _(b)_ Minimum grid spacing versus $N$ for the three grids: standard $cal(O)(1 / N^2)$ scaling, aggressive $cal(O)(1 / N)$. _(c)_ Spectral radius of the first-derivative matrix; aggressive KTE reduces stiffness by nearly an order of magnitude at $N = 96$. _(d)_ Chebyshev coefficient $|a_N|$ of $f(y) = y$ sampled on each grid, with the theoretical asymptote $0.488 / N^2$ (navy dotted) confirming Boyd's analysis: aggressive KTE destroys geometric convergence for the simplest polynomial, while conservative KTE preserves it down to the floating-point floor. The four panels read top-down as the trade-off itself: panel (a) sets the geometry, (b) and (c) collect its operator-level wins (smaller spacing, smaller stiffness), and (d) collects the accuracy loss. The conservative choice is the only one that wins everywhere.
Alt Text: Four panels on the Kosloff-Tal-Ezer map trade-off between accuracy and timestep. Panel a plots the map for three regimes: standard Chebyshev as the straight identity, aggressive beta near one over N squared which is nearly straight, and conservative beta retaining a clear S-shape, with input nodes as ticks along the bottom. Panel b plots minimum grid spacing versus N on a log-log axis, standard scaling like one over N squared and aggressive like the gentler one over N. Panel c plots the spectral radius of the first-derivative matrix versus N, aggressive KTE cutting stiffness by nearly an order of magnitude at N of ninety-six. Panel d plots the Chebyshev coefficient magnitude of f equals y versus N on a log-log axis with a theoretical 0.488 over N squared asymptote; aggressive KTE follows this algebraic decay, destroying geometric convergence, while conservative KTE drops to the floating-point floor and preserves it.

Caption: Étude 20.3: sinc expansion of $sech(y)$. _(a)_: error versus $h$ at fixed $N = 48$; the V-shape exhibits the trade-off between bandwidth error (left branch) and grid-span error (right branch), with the empirical optimum (navy dotted) and the theoretical $sqrt(pi^2 / (2 N))$ (teal dashed) agreeing tightly. _(b)_: the literal _two masters_ decomposition --- bandwidth error $E_W (h) tilde.op (4 / pi) e^(-pi^2 / (2 h))$ (navy dashed) and grid-span error $E_("DT")(N h) tilde.op 4 e^(-N h / 2)$ (coral dashed) shown separately, with their sum (teal solid) recovering the empirical V (grey); the two analytic curves cross at the empirical $h^star$. _(c)_: max-norm error vs $sqrt(N)$ at the optimal $h$; the curve is straight on this scale, confirming the subgeometric rate $exp(-pi sqrt(N / 2))$ (navy dotted guide). _(d)_: grid cartoon at $N = 8$ and $N = 32$ --- as $N$ quadruples, the span doubles _and_ the spacing halves.

Caption: Étude 21.7: Ioakimidis non-iterative root for $f(x) = sin(x - pi / 4) / sqrt(1 + 10 x^2)$ on $[-1, 1]$ (the unique root is $rho = pi / 4 approx 0.7853981633974483$). The Ioakimidis formulaIoakimidis formula has *no iteration anywhere* --- it is a single quotient of two finite sums.

Chapter: afterword.typ
Caption: Comparison of collocation (pseudospectral) and pure Galerkin spectral methods.
Alt Text: A five-row comparison table contrasting the collocation (pseudospectral) and pure Galerkin spectral approaches across the key design dimensions that distinguish them: collocation enforces the residual pointwise at discrete nodes, evaluates nonlinear terms by pointwise multiplication in physical space, yields dense non-symmetric differentiation matrices, imposes boundary conditions explicitly through matrix surgery, and rests on discrete quadrature bounds for stability; the Galerkin method instead enforces global orthogonality through an integral inner product, handles nonlinearities via convolution of coefficients, produces often symmetric, sparse, or banded matrices, satisfies boundary conditions implicitly through the design of the basis functions, and gains stability guarantees from continuous coercivity and energy norms. The takeaway is that collocation buys implementation simplicity and easy treatment of nonlinearities at the cost of dense, ill-conditioned operators, whereas Galerkin trades pointwise convenience for sparse, well-structured operators and rigorous stability.
